fields.meta_description: Screen each applicant, nudge slow hiring managers, and hold offers above the pay band with recruitment automation you build in Emergent.
fields.h1: Build Recruitment Automation That Moves Every Candidate
fields.hero_description: Build recruitment automation that screens every applicant and keeps each candidate moving toward an offer.
fields.features_subheading: Your recruiting workflow becomes an app where each step has an owner and a time limit, and nobody has to chase a hiring manager.
fields.feature_1:
Applications screened on arrival

Each application is checked against the knockout questions you set, such as a required license or a shift the role needs. Anyone who misses one goes to a queue a recruiter reviews.
fields.feature_2:
A time limit on every stage

Set how long a candidate may wait at each step. Once that time passes, the owner hears about it in Slack or by email, with every waiting candidate listed by days waited.
fields.feature_3:
Past finalists found when a role reopens

When a requisition opens again, the app searches candidates who reached the final round for it and lists them for the recruiter with the notes from their last interview.
fields.feature_4:
Offers checked against the pay band

Before a letter is drafted, each offer is compared with the band for its role and level. An amount above the maximum waits for the approver you name, who decides in Slack.
fields.feature_5:
Synced with your applicant tracking system

Candidates, stages, and offers sync with Greenhouse or any applicant tracking system with an API. Recruiters keep working in the views they know while the app runs the rules.
fields.feature_6:
Hiring rules as code you own

Every knockout question and time limit is readable code that you can export to your GitHub repository on paid plans. Candidate records sit in a database your team owns.
fields.why_description: Emergent shapes your hiring workflow around your own stages and pay bands, as an app your team owns and changes by prompting.

fields.tab_content_1:
184 applicants, and 123 move on to a phone screen

Orchard Lane Clinics got 184 applications for a medical assistant opening in a week. Two knockout questions ask for CPR certification and Saturday availability. The 61 who answered no to either wait in a decline queue that recruiter Dana Whitfield reads before any email goes out. The other 123 go to her phone screen.
fields.tab_content_2:
Nine days in review, and Dr. Park hears about it

Candidates lose interest while a hiring manager holds them in review. Any candidate who waits more than five business days in that stage is flagged. Dr. Elena Park, who runs the Eastgate clinic, gets one Slack message listing her four waiting candidates, the oldest at nine days, with a link to each profile.
fields.tab_content_3:
Three finalists from last year get the first call

Orchard Lane's front desk coordinator role opens again every few months. This time the app searched for candidates who reached the final interview for it in the last 12 months and found three, each with the interviewer's notes attached. Dana writes to them before the job is posted publicly.
fields.tab_content_4:
Offers above the pay band go to the COO first

The clinic manager band at Orchard Lane tops out at $84,000, and the hiring team wants to offer $88,000. That puts the offer $4,000 over the maximum. The letter is not drafted until COO Ray Okafor approves the amount in a direct Slack message or sends it back to the team.

fields.howto_description: Seven steps to build recruitment automation that screens applicants and keeps every hiring stage moving, tested on past applicants first.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Write knockout questions as yes or no
fields.howto_step_1_des: Map the steps a candidate passes through: applied, phone screen, hiring manager review, interview, offer. Give each stage one owner and a time limit in business days. A stage with no owner is where candidates stall.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write each knockout question as a yes or no about a hard requirement, such as CPR certification for a clinical job. Keep the list short. Anything that needs judgment, such as years of experience, belongs in the recruiter's screen.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Import the minimum and maximum pay for each role and level, then name who approves an offer above the maximum. Emergent builds the check against that table. Compensation can update a band later without anyone rewriting the approval logic.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Connect Greenhouse or the ATS your team already uses through its API. Candidates and stage changes sync in, and decisions made in the app write back. Recruiters keep their usual screens while the rules run against the same records.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Choose who gets each reminder and where it lands. One Slack digest a day per hiring manager is easier to act on than a ping for every candidate. Recruiters may want decline reviews by email instead. Set it per stage and change it by prompting.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Send last month's applicants through the app before launch. Compare each knockout decision and stage reminder with what your recruiters did by hand. Where they differ, adjust the rule by prompting and run the batch again until the two agree.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Go live with one busy role
fields.howto_step_7_des: Turn the app on for your highest-volume opening first, and keep a recruiter reading every decline for two weeks. Once the queue holds no surprises, add the next role and its hiring workflow, then switch on the offer check.
fields.hero_prompt: Build recruitment automation that screens applicants and tracks every hiring stage for my clinic group.

plan.angle: The top 10 are explainers and tool roundups (IBM, Gem, Greenhouse, Recruiterflow, People Managing People) that list what recruitment automation can do in general terms. This page shows the hiring team at one clinic group running it: knockout questions that sort 184 applications with a recruiter checking every decline, a hiring manager nudged about candidates stuck in review, past finalists surfaced when a role reopens, and an offer over its pay band sent to the COO before it goes out. Interview scheduling and onboarding are left to their sibling pages.
tab_stories: Orchard Lane Clinics gets 184 applications for a medical assistant opening in a week, and the 61 who answer no to a required CPR certification or Saturday shifts move to a decline queue that recruiter Dana Whitfield reads before any email goes out.
Any candidate who sits in hiring manager review for more than five business days is flagged, and Dr. Elena Park gets one Slack message listing her four waiting candidates, the oldest at nine days.
When the front desk coordinator role reopens, the app finds the three people who reached the final interview for it in the last 12 months and drafts a note for the recruiter to send each one.
An $88,000 offer for a clinic manager sits $4,000 above the $84,000 top of the pay band, so it waits for COO Ray Okafor to approve in Slack before the offer letter is drafted.
